items.title: StateAlign: Internalizing State-Aware Decision-Making for Reliable Multi-Turn Tool Agents via Reinforcement Learning
items.summary_1line: Reinforcement learning has improved the tool-use capabilities of large language models. However, better task performance can coincide with increased tool hallucination. Reliable tool use requires decisions to follow the current task state: available information, tool capabilities
items.editor_note: Adds a failure mode to the agent-training strand: RL tool-use gains can coincide with more tool hallucination, so it trains decisions to follow the current task state.

items.title: AutoRL: A Multi-Agent System towards Autonomous Reinforcement Learning

items.title: Imitation Bootstrapped Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

editorial.tldr: This thread is a topical grouping of 23 arXiv preprints since Oct 27, not one event: what they share is reinforcement learning as a post-training method for LLMs and agents. Most work on one of three problems: what the reward should measure, how to train multi-turn tool-using agents, and how to pay for the rollouts.
editorial.whats_new: Nov 13 adds AutoRL, a multi-agent system proposed to run the full RL training pipeline itself, and a method that bootstraps multi-agent RL from demonstrations; the Nov 12 StateAlign finding that RL tool-use gains can raise tool hallucination stays the main practical flag.
editorial.why_it_matters: For teams that post-train their own agents, these papers flag three costs: rollout scheduling as an infrastructure problem, reward design, and RL tool-use gains that can bring more tool hallucination.
editorial.take_for_builders: Before adding GPUs to an agent RL pipeline, measure how much rollout wall-clock goes to environment execution and padding; after any RL tool-use tune, track tool-hallucination rate alongside task success.

beats.headline: Outcome-only rewards draw four papers on calibration, guidance and self-learning
beats.summary: These papers change what the policy is rewarded for: matching confidence to correctness, or using the textual feedback and hints a single outcome score discards.

beats.headline: RL moves onto the agent stack: harnesses, skills, memory and sub-agents
beats.summary: Nine papers apply RL to parts of an agent system rather than to a single-turn model; one asks what multi-turn RL actually improves, and one targets the tool hallucination RL can introduce.

beats.headline: Two papers treat rollout scheduling as the bottleneck
beats.summary: Environment-aware scheduling under a finite rollout budget on Oct 27, and an offline scheduler for asynchronous LLM RL on Nov 6.

beats.headline: AutoRL proposes agents that run the RL pipeline themselves
beats.summary: The newest agent-side entry flips the direction: instead of RL training an agent, a multi-agent system is pitched to carry out the RL training loop.

beats.headline: Seven clustered papers sit outside LLM agent post-training
beats.summary: Diffusion and flow fine-tuning, classical RL interpretability and theory, world-model memory, and demonstration-bootstrapped multi-agent RL.

open_questions: Do either of the two rollout-scheduling approaches ship as open-source code or get adopted in a public training stack?
Does an independent group reproduce the finding that multi-turn RL gains depend on sampling breadth and interaction depth?
Do the confidence-calibration methods for RLVR hold on agent tasks, beyond the reasoning settings they were proposed for?
Does co-evolving the harness with the policy beat tuning a harness for a fixed policy on a shared public benchmark?
Does state-aware RL training cut tool hallucination without giving back the task-success gains, on a public multi-turn tool benchmark?
Does AutoRL report end-to-end runs where its agents produce a trained policy that beats a human-configured RL baseline?
